Scripture supports this doctrine through several key lines of reasoning: the preserving power of God, the certainty of His purpose, and the enduring nature of the New Covenant.

Here are the primary biblical texts used to support this doctrine, categorized by theme.

### 1. The Keeping Power of God
The strongest biblical argument for perseverance is that salvation is not maintained by human effort, but by divine power.

*   **John 10:27–30**
    > "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and **no one will snatch them out of my hand**. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand. I and the Father are one."
    *   *The Argument:* Jesus promises that "no one" (external forces or internal failure) can snatch a believer from the hands of the Father and the Son. The security is based on the strength of the Shepherd, not the sheep.

    *   *The Argument:* Believers are "guarded" by God’s power. The Greek word for "guarded" (*phroureō*) implies a military garrison or protection, indicating that God actively protects the believer’s faith.

*   **Jude 1:24**
    > "Now to him who is able to **keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless** before the presence of his glory with great joy..."
    *   *The Argument:* The assurance of standing blameless before God is attributed to God’s ability to "keep" the believer, not the believer’s ability to hold on.

### 2. The Certainty of God’s Purpose (Election)
Scripture teaches that God’s decree of election cannot be thwarted. If God chose a people for Himself, He will surely bring them to glory.

questions.question: What verses support the doctrine of total depravity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:10-12, Eph 2:1-3, Gen 6:5
questions.response:
The doctrine of **Total Depravity** is the first of the Five Points of Calvinism (TULIP). It teaches that, as a result of the Fall, every part of the human person—mind, will, emotions, and body—has been corrupted by sin. It does not mean that people are as evil as they could possibly be, but that sin affects the *whole* person, rendering them unable to turn to God or choose salvation without divine intervention.

Here are the primary biblical verses used to support this doctrine, categorized by the specific aspect of the doctrine they address.

### 1. The Universality of Sin
These verses establish that sin is not an isolated act but a universal condition affecting every human being (except Jesus Christ).

*   **Romans 3:10–12:** "As it is written: 'There is no one righteous, not even one; there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God. All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.'"
    *   *Support:* This passage argues that the lack of righteousness is total ("not even one") and that the natural human state is one of actively turning away from God.
*   **Romans 3:23:** "For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
*   **1 Kings 8:46:** "...for there is no one who does not sin..."
*   **Ecclesiastes 7:20:** "Indeed, there is no one on earth who is righteous, no one who does what is right and never sins."

### 2. The Corruption of the Heart and Mind
These verses support the idea that the "inner person"—the intellect and the desires—is fundamentally bent toward evil.

*   **Genesis 6:5:** "The Lord saw how great the wickedness of the human race had become on the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil all the time."
    *   *Support:* This highlights that the corruption is internal (thoughts/heart) and constant ("all the time").
*   **Jeremiah 17:9:** "The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?"
    *   *Support:* The Hebrew word for "beyond cure" (*anus*) implies an incurable sickness, suggesting humans cannot fix their own spiritual condition.
*   **Ephesians 4:17–18:** "So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord, that you must no longer live as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking. They are darkened in their understanding and separated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them due to the hardening of their hearts."
*   **Titus 1:15:** "To the pure, all things are pure, but to those who are corrupted and do not believe, nothing is pure. In fact, both their minds and consciences are corrupted."

### 3. The Bondage of the Will (Inability)
A key component of Total Depravity is that humans are not just sick, but spiritually dead, meaning they lack the moral ability to choose God or do true spiritual good on their own.

*   **John 6:44:** "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws them, and I will raise them up at the last day."
    *   *Support:* The word "can" (*dunamai*) refers to ability, not permission. It suggests an inherent inability to come to Christ without divine action.
*   **John 6:65:** "He went on to say, 'This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless the Father has enabled them.'"
*   **Romans 8:7–8:** "The mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God; it does not submit to God’s law, nor can it do so. Those who are in the realm of the flesh cannot please God."
    *   *Support:* This argues that the unsaved person ("flesh") is not just unwilling, but *unable* ("cannot") to submit to God's law.
*   **Ephesians 2:1–3:** "As for you, you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you used to live when you followed the ways of this world..."
    *   *Support:* The metaphor of death implies total passivity. A corpse cannot raise itself; similarly, a spiritually dead person cannot choose to be made alive without God's intervention.
*   **1 Corinthians 2:14:** "The person without the Spirit does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God but considers them foolishness, and cannot understand them because they are discerned only through the Spirit."
    *   *Support:* This speaks to the "noetic effects of sin"—that sin has blinded the mind to spiritual truth.

### 4. Original Sin and Human Nature
These verses support the idea that humans are born with a sinful nature; sin is inherited, not just learned behavior.

*   **Psalm 51:5:** "Surely I was sinful at birth, sinful from the time my mother conceived me."
*   **Psalm 58:3:** "Even from birth the wicked go astray; from the womb they are wayward, spreading lies."
*   **Romans 5:12:** "Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and in this way death came to all people, because all sinned..."

### 5. The Need for Regeneration
If humans could choose God on their own, a "new birth" would not be necessary. These verses imply that God must change the nature before a person can believe.

*   **John 3:3:** "Jesus replied, 'Very truly I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again.'"
*   **Ezekiel 36:26:** "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh."
    *   *Support:* This portrays salvation as a unilateral act of God replacing a "heart of stone" (an organ unable to respond) with a living heart.

### Summary of the Argument
Proponents of Total Depravity synthesize these verses to argue that:
1.  Sin affects every person (Universality).
2.  Sin affects every part of the person (Totality).
3.  Sin renders a person unable to save themselves (Inability).
4.  Therefore, salvation must be initiated and completed by God's grace (Monergism).

questions.question: Which passages teach justification by faith alone?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:28, Eph 2:8-9, Gal 2:16
questions.response:
The doctrine of **justification by faith alone** (often referred to by the Latin term *Sola Fide*) is primarily derived from the writings of the Apostle Paul in the New Testament, though it is rooted in the example of Abraham in the Old Testament.

Here are the key passages that are historically cited as the primary biblical basis for this teaching, categorized by their theological emphasis.

### 1. The Core Theological Statements (Romans & Galatians)
These passages provide the most explicit arguments that right standing with God is achieved through faith, not by observing the Law or performing "works."

**Romans 3:28**
> "For we maintain that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law." (NIV)
*   *Significance:* This is perhaps the clearest statement of the doctrine. Paul creates a direct contrast between "faith" and "works of the law," asserting that justification (being declared righteous) is distinct from human effort.

**Galatians 2:16**
> "Know that a person is not justified by the works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ. So we, too, have put our faith in Christ Jesus that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, because by the works of the law no one will be justified."
*   *Significance:* Paul repeats the concept three times in a single verse, emphasizing that neither Jewish Christians nor Gentiles can achieve justification through legal obedience.

**Romans 5:1**
> "Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."
*   *Significance:* This passage highlights the result of justification by faith: a restored relationship (peace) with God, accessible only through faith, not through personal merit.

### 2. The Example of Abraham (The Old Testament Foundation)
Paul argues that this doctrine is not new but was always God's method of saving people, using Abraham as the prime example.

**Genesis 15:6**
> "Abram believed the Lord, and he credited it to him as righteousness."
*   *Significance:* This is the foundational Old Testament text. Before Abraham performed any religious acts (like circumcision) or works of the law, his belief was "credited" (imputed) to him as righteousness.

**Romans 4:2–5**
> "If, in fact, Abraham was justified by works, he had something to boast about—but not before God. What does Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.' Now to the one who works, wages are not credited as a gift but as an obligation. However, to the one who does not work but trusts God who justifies the ungodly, their faith is credited as righteousness."

While the term "Original Sin" is a theological construct developed later in church history (notably by Augustine), the doctrine is derived from a specific narrative arc throughout Scripture.

Here are the key Scripture passages that establish this doctrine, categorized by their theological contribution.

### 1. The Origin: The Fall of Humanity
The foundation of the doctrine is the historical event where sin entered the human experience.

*   **Genesis 3:6–7** (The Act of Disobedience)
    > *“So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food... she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate. Then the eyes of both were opened...”*

    *   **Significance:** The penalties for sin—pain, toil, and death—were not limited to Adam and Eve but extended to their environment and progeny, suggesting a cosmic and generational impact.

### 2. The Inherited Nature: The Old Testament Witness

*   **Psalm 51:5**
    > *“Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.”*
    *   **Significance:** This is arguably the strongest Old testament evidence for Original Sin. David is not claiming his mother sinned in conceiving him, but rather that he himself was sinful from the very moment of conception. This points to a condition, not just an action.

*   **Psalm 58:3**

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of the Trinity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14, John 1:1, Gen 1:26
questions.response:
The doctrine of the Trinity—that there is **one God** who exists in **three distinct persons** (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit)—is not found in a single verse of the Bible. Instead, it is a systematic theology derived from the totality of Scripture.

The Bible teaches the doctrine through a logical progression of three biblical truths: **Monotheism** (there is one God), the **Deity of Three** (the Father, Son, and Spirit are each God), and **Distinction** (they are distinct persons).

Here is where the Bible teaches each component of the doctrine.

### 1. The Bible Teaches There is Only One God (Monotheism)
The foundation of the Trinity is that there is only one divine essence. The Bible is strictly monotheistic.

*   **Deuteronomy 6:4:** "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one." (The *Shema*, the central declaration of Jewish faith).
*   **Isaiah 45:5:** "I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no God."
*   **1 Corinthians 8:4:** "...We know that 'An idol is nothing at all in the world' and that 'There is no God but one.'"
*   **1 Timothy 2:5:** "For there is one God..."

### 2. The Bible Teaches that the Father, Son, and Spirit are God
If the Bible only taught monotheism, we would have simple Unitarianism. However, the New Testament clearly identifies three distinct entities as possessing the nature of God.

**The Father is God**
This is the least contested point in Scripture.
*   **1 Corinthians 8:6:** "...Yet for us there is but one God, the Father..."
*   **John 17:3:** Jesus prays, "Now this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God..."

**The Son (Jesus) is God**
The New Testament affirms the full deity of Christ.
*   **John 1:1:** "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." (Verse 14 clarifies that "the Word became flesh" in Jesus).
*   **John 20:28:** Thomas sees the resurrected Jesus and calls him, "My Lord and my God!"
*   **Colossians 2:9:** "For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form."
*   **Hebrews 1:8:** The Father says of the Son, "Your throne, O God, will last for ever and ever."

**The Holy Spirit is God**
The Spirit is not presented as an impersonal force, but as a divine person.
*   **Acts 5:3-4:** Peter confronts Ananias: "You have lied to the Holy Spirit... You have not lied just to human beings but to God." (Equating lying to the Spirit with lying to God).
*   **1 Corinthians 3:16:** "Don’t you know that you yourselves are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in your midst?"
*   **Hebrews 9:14:** The Spirit is described as "eternal," an attribute belonging only to God.

### 3. The Bible Teaches Distinction of Persons
The Bible shows that the Father, Son, and Spirit are not just different names for the same person (Modalism), but relate to one another distinctively.

*   **The Baptism of Jesus (Matthew 3:16-17):** In one scene, all three persons are present and active simultaneously. The Son is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven.
*   **The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19):** "Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." The singular "name" implies unity, while the three persons imply distinction.
*   **Jesus’ Prayer (John 17):** Jesus (the Son) prays to the Father. This demonstrates a relationship between two distinct persons, not one person talking to himself.
*   **John 15:26:** Jesus says, "When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth who goes out from the Father—he will testify about me." Here, the Son sends the Spirit from the Father, showing distinct roles and origins.

### Summary: How These Form the Doctrine
The doctrine of the Trinity is the theological conclusion drawn from holding these three biblical truths together simultaneously:

1.  There is **one** God (Isaiah 45:5).
2.  The **Father** is God, the **Son** is God, and the **Spirit** is God (John 1:1; Acts 5:3-4).
3.  The Father, Son, and Spirit are **distinct** from one another (Matthew 3:16-17).

Therefore, the one God of the Bible exists eternally in three co-equal, co-eternal persons.

### Historical Note
While the doctrine is biblical, the word "Trinity" does not appear in the Bible. The term was coined by the early church father Tertullian (c. 155–240 AD) to summarize this biblical data. The doctrine was formally codified at the Council of Nicaea (325 AD) and the Council of Constantinople (381 AD) to defend the biblical teaching against views that claimed Jesus was a created being (Arianism) or that God was just one person wearing different masks (Modalism).

questions.question: Which Bible passages teach the bodily resurrection of Christ?

questions.response:
The bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ is a central doctrine of the Christian faith. The Bible teaches that Jesus was not raised as a disembodied spirit or a ghost, but in a glorified, physical body that could be seen, touched, and that could consume food.

Here are the key passages that teach the bodily resurrection, categorized by the type of evidence they provide.

    *   **Key Point:** Jesus explicitly distinguishes Himself from a spirit by declaring He has "flesh and bones" and proving it by eating physical food.

### 2. The Empty Tomb and Grave Clothes
The Gospels emphasize that Jesus' body was not just revitalized and then left the tomb; the physical body was transformed and vacated the tomb, leaving the physical evidence behind.

*   **John 20:6–7**
    > "...He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus' head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself."
    *   **Key Point:** The presence of the grave clothes suggests the body was not stolen (a thief would not unwrap and fold a body) but physically transformed and exited the linen.
*   **Matthew 28:6**
    > "He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay."
    *   **Key Point:** The angel points to the physical vacancy of the tomb where the body had been laid.

### 3. Physical Touch and Examination
The resurrection accounts record multiple instances where people physically touched Jesus, proving He was not a hallucination or an apparition.

*   **John 20:27–29 (The Doubting Thomas Account)**
    > "Then he said to Thomas, 'Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.'"
    *   **Key Point:** Jesus invites Thomas to physically verify the wounds in His body. The resurrection body retains the physical marks of the crucifixion.
*   **Matthew 28:9**
    > "And behold, Jesus met them, saying, 'Greetings!' And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him."
    *   **Key Point:** The women "took hold" (grasped) His feet, an action impossible for a spirit or a hallucination.

### 4. Apostolic Preaching in Acts

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the imputation of Christ's righteousness?

questions.response:
The doctrine of the imputation of Christ’s righteousness is a central tenet of Reformed and Protestant theology. It teaches that justification is not a process of making a person internally righteous, but a legal (forensic) declaration in which the perfect obedience and righteousness of Jesus Christ are credited to the believer’s account.

The Bible teaches this through specific keywords (like "impute" or "count") and through theological arguments contrasting Adam and Christ. Here are the primary biblical texts where this doctrine is established.

### 1. The "Great Exchange" (2 Corinthians 5:21)
This is arguably the most explicit verse regarding the double imputation (our sin to Christ, Christ's righteousness to us).

> *"For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God."* (ESV)

*   **The teaching:** Paul presents a divine exchange. Christ had no sin of his own; he "became sin" by bearing the legal liability and guilt of his people (imputation of sin). Conversely, believers—who are not inherently righteous in themselves—"become the righteousness of God." This is not an infusion of personal holiness, but a change in legal standing before God.

### 2. The Adam/Christ Parallel (Romans 5:12–19)
In this passage, Paul establishes the principle of "federal headship"—that one person can represent many, and the actions of that one person are credited to the group.

> *"Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous."* (Romans 5:18–19)

*   **The teaching:** Just as Adam’s sin was imputed (credited) to the human race resulting in condemnation, Christ’s "one act of righteousness" (his life of obedience and sacrificial death) is imputed to his people, resulting in justification.
*   The phrase "made righteous" (Greek: *kathistēmi*) in verse 19 does not refer to moral transformation (sanctification) but to a status change, just as being "made sinners" by Adam refers to a status of guilt rather than a change in Adam's nature.

### 3. The Logic of Imputation (Romans 4:1–8)
Paul uses the example of Abraham to explain how righteousness is credited apart from works.

> *"Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness... Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness."* (Romans 4:3–5)

Here are the key passages that describe the **process** of sanctification, categorized by how they explain the work being done.

### 1. The Role of God’s Word and Truth
Scripture presents the Word of God as the primary tool the Holy Spirit uses to cleanse and change the believer.

*   **Ephesians 5:25–26**
    > *"Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word."*
    **The Process:** Here, sanctification is likened to a cleansing bath. The "washing" suggests a progressive removal of spiritual defilement through the regular application of Scripture.

### 2. The Role of the Holy Spirit
Sanctification is not merely self-improvement; it is a spiritual work empowered by God.

*   **2 Corinthians 3:18**
    > *"And we all, who with unveiled faces contemplate the Lord’s glory, are being transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit."*
    **The Process:** This is one of the clearest verses on progressive sanctification. The phrase "ever-increasing glory" indicates a gradual movement toward Christlikeness. It happens as we "contemplate" (behold) Christ.
*   **Romans 15:16**
    > *"…to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. He gave me the priestly duty of proclaiming the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit."*
    **The Process:** Paul attributes the sanctification of the Gentiles to the work of the Spirit, showing that the result of gospel proclamation is a people set apart by God's power.

### 3. The Believer’s Active Participation (Synergy)
While God works in the believer, the believer is commanded to "work out" that holiness. These passages emphasize human responsibility in the process.

*   **Philippians 2:12–13**
    > *"Therefore, my dear friends, as you have always obeyed—not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence—continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you to will and to act in order to fulfill his good purpose."*

questions.question: What Bible passages support covenant theology?

Covenant Theology is a framework for understanding Scripture that views the relationship between God and humanity as structured through a series of theological covenants. Proponents of Covenant Theology generally identify three overarching theological covenants: the **Covenant of Redemption** (within the Trinity), the **Covenant of Works** (with Adam), and the **Covenant of Grace** (with Christ and the elect).

Here are the key Bible passages used to support these distinct aspects of Covenant Theology.

### 1. The Covenant of Works (Adamic Covenant)

    *   **Support:** While the word "covenant" is not used here, Covenant Theologians argue that the elements of a covenant are present: a stipulation (don't eat), a penalty (death), and an implied reward (life, symbolized by the Tree of Life).
*   **Hosea 6:7** – *"But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me."*
    *   **Support:** This is a crucial proof text. The phrase "like Adam" (or "at Adam," depending on translation) suggests that Adam was in a covenant relationship that he broke, just as Israel broke their covenant later.
*   **Romans 5:12–19** – *"Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin... For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous."*
    *   **Support:** This passage establishes the principle of **Federal Headship**. Adam acted as a representative for the human race. His "disobedience" is contrasted with Christ's "obedience," implying a parallel covenant structure (Works vs. Grace).

### 2. The Covenant of Grace
After the Fall, God initiated a covenant of grace, promising salvation through the seed of the woman. Covenant Theology teaches that this single covenant underlies all subsequent biblical covenants (Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New).

*   **Genesis 3:15** – *"I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."*

questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the Lord's Supper (also known as Communion or the Eucharist) primarily in the New Testament. The teachings can be categorized into three main groups: the **institution narratives** (where it started), the **theological instructions** (how to observe it), and the **historical practices** of the early church.

Here are the key passages where the Bible teaches about the Lord's Supper:

### 1. The Institution Narratives (The Gospels)
The first three Gospels record the exact moment Jesus established the practice during the Passover meal (the Last Supper) before His crucifixion.

*   **Matthew 26:26–29:** Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to the disciples, saying, "Take, eat; this is my body." He then takes the cup, saying, "Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant."
*   **Mark 14:22–25:** A parallel account to Matthew, emphasizing the covenant aspect and Jesus' refusal to drink of the fruit of the vine again until that day when He drinks it new in the kingdom of God.
*   **Luke 22:14–23:** Luke provides the most detailed account, mentioning two cups. It includes the key phrase often used in church liturgy: "Do this in remembrance of me."

### 2. The Theological Instructions (The Epistles)
The Apostle Paul provides the most in-depth theological explanation and practical instructions for the church.

*   **1 Corinthians 11:17–34:** This is arguably the most important passage for understanding the *purpose* and *manner* of the Lord's Supper.
    *   **Verses 23–26:** Paul recounts the institution, stating that he received this from the Lord. He emphasizes that the act proclaims the Lord's death until He comes.
    *   **Verses 27–32:** Paul warns against taking the supper in an "unworthy manner." He instructs believers to "examine themselves" before eating and drinking, distinguishing between the physical act and the spiritual reality of discerning the body of Christ.
*   **1 Corinthians 10:14–22:** Paul uses the Lord's Supper to argue against idolatry. He explains that the cup is a "participation" (or fellowship) in the blood of Christ and the bread is a participation in the body of Christ. He argues that because we share in Christ through this meal, we cannot share in the table of demons.

### 3. The Spiritual Foundation (The Gospel of John)
While John does not record the institution of the supper, he records Jesus' teaching that provides the theological background for it.

*   **John 6:25–59 (The Bread of Life Discourse):** Jesus teaches, "I am the bread of life." He tells the crowd, "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life." This passage is often interpreted as the spiritual reality that the physical act of Communion represents.

### 4. The Practice of the Early Church (Acts)
The book of Acts shows how the early Christians implemented this teaching immediately after the resurrection.

*   **Acts 2:42:** The early church "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers." "Breaking bread" is widely understood to refer to the Lord's Supper.
*   **Acts 20:7:** Luke notes, "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread..." This indicates that the early church observed the supper weekly on Sundays (the day of resurrection).

### Summary of Biblical Themes
Across these passages, the Bible teaches four main things about the Lord's Supper:
1.  **Commemoration:** It is a memorial to remember Christ’s death ("Do this in remembrance of me").
2.  **Proclamation:** It is a public announcement of the Gospel ("You proclaim the Lord's death until He comes").
3.  **Participation:** It is a spiritual union with Christ ("Participation in the body and blood").
4.  **Expectation:** It looks forward to the future return of Jesus ("Until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom").

questions.question: What passages address the doctrine of baptism?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4, Col 2:11-12
questions.response:
The doctrine of baptism is addressed throughout the New Testament, with foundational types found in the Old Testament. The passages can be categorized by the theological themes they present, such as the command to baptize, the mode, the meaning, and its relationship to salvation.

Here are the key passages addressing the doctrine of baptism, categorized by theme.

### 1. The Great Commission (The Command)
These passages establish baptism as an ordinance of the church and a command for believers.

*   **Matthew 28:19–20** – "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you."
    *   *Significance:* This establishes the Trinitarian formula for baptism and links it directly to discipleship.
*   **Mark 16:16** – "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned."
    *   *Significance:* This passage links faith and baptism, though theological traditions differ on the nature of that link.

### 2. Baptism and Salvation / Repentance
The Book of Acts contains the historical record of the early church practicing baptism, often connecting it closely with repentance and the forgiveness of sins.

*   **Acts 2:38** – "And Peter said to them, 'Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'"
    *   *Significance:* This is the first sermon of the church age. It connects baptism to repentance, forgiveness, and the reception of the Holy Spirit.
*   **Acts 22:16** – "And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name."
    *   *Significance:* Ananias speaks to Paul, using the imagery of "washing away sins" in connection with baptism.
*   **1 Peter 3:21** – "Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ."
    *   *Significance:* This is one of the most explicit theological statements regarding what baptism does ("now saves you"), though Peter clarifies it is not a physical washing but a spiritual appeal/pledge.

### 3. Baptism as Identification with Christ (Theology of Paul)
Paul’s epistles explain the spiritual meaning of baptism, focusing on the believer’s union with Christ in his death and resurrection.

*   **Romans 6:3–4** – "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life."
    *   *Significance:* This is the primary passage for the doctrine of "Regeneration" or "Union with Christ." It portrays baptism as a symbolic burial and resurrection.
*   **Galatians 3:27** – "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ."
    *   *Significance:* Baptism is described as "putting on" Christ, signifying a change in identity and status.
*   **Colossians 2:11–12** – "In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism..."
    *   *Significance:* Paul connects baptism to Old Testament circumcision, providing a theological link between the Old Covenant sign and the New Covenant sign.

### 4. Baptism of the Holy Spirit vs. Water Baptism
Some passages distinguish between ritual water baptism and the spiritual baptism of the Holy Spirit.

*   **Acts 1:5** – "For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now."
*   **1 Corinthians 12:13** – "For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit."
    *   *Significance:* This speaks to the spiritual reality that places a believer into the universal church body, distinct from (though often accompanied by) water baptism.

### 5. Accounts of Baptism (Mode and Subjects)
The narratives in Acts provide insight into *how* and *who* was baptized.

*   **Jesus’ Baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)**: Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan River. The Father speaks from heaven, endorsing the event.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about church government and eldership?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Tim 3:1-7, Titus 1:5-9, Acts 14:23, 1 Pet 5:1-4
questions.response:
Scripture does not provide a single, detailed manual for church government (like a modern constitution), but it does provide clear instructions, qualifications, and examples regarding leadership structure. The New Testament presents a model often described as "elder-led" or "plurality of elders," supported by deacons and congregational involvement.

Here are the primary biblical texts that teach on church government and eldership, categorized by theme.

### 1. The Terminology: Elder, Overseer, and Pastor
In the New Testament, the terms **Elder** (*Presbyteros*), **Overseer** (*Episkopos*, often translated Bishop), and **Pastor** (*Poimen*, meaning Shepherd) are used interchangeably to refer to the same office.

*   **Acts 20:17–38:** This is a crucial passage. Paul summons the **"elders"** (v. 17) of the church in Ephesus. In his address to them, he says, "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you **overseers**" (v. 28). He then commands them to "shepherd" (pastor) the church of God.
    *   *Key takeaway:* An elder is an overseer who functions as a pastor/shepherd.
*   **1 Peter 5:1–4:** Peter writes to the **"elders"** among them, urging them to "shepherd the flock of God" and to exercise "oversight."
    *   *Key takeaway:* The three terms describe one function: an elder exercises oversight and shepherding.
*   **Titus 1:5–7:** Paul tells Titus to "appoint **elders** in every town." He then immediately describes the qualifications of an "elder" and switches to the term "**overseer**" in verse 7 without distinction.

### 2. The Qualifications for Elders
Scripture provides two primary lists of qualifications for those serving in this office. These passages emphasize character and home management over specific giftedness.

*   **1 Timothy 3:1–7:** "The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task." Paul lists qualifications including being "above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable... not a drunkard... not quarrelsome."
*   **Titus 1:5–9:** Similar to Timothy, this passage emphasizes holding firm to the trustworthy word so that he may "give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it."

questions.question: What Bible passages teach about the second coming of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Acts 1:11, 1 Thess 4:16-17, Matt 24:30, Rev 1:7
questions.response:

Here are the key Bible passages regarding the Second Coming, categorized by where they are found and what they emphasize.

### 1. The Teachings of Jesus
Jesus spoke extensively about His return, emphasizing that it would be visible, sudden, and unexpected.

*   **Matthew 24:30–31 (The Sign of the Son of Man)**
    > "Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see 'the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven' with power and great glory. And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other."
    *   *Key Theme:* Visibility ("every eye will see Him"), power, and the gathering of believers.

*   **Matthew 25:31–32 (The Judgment of the Nations)**
    > "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory. All the nations will be gathered before him..."
    *   *Key Theme:* The Second Coming is directly linked to final judgment and the establishment of His kingdom.

*   **John 14:1–3 (The Promise to Return)**
    > "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places... I go to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also."
    *   *Key Theme:* Comfort and the personal reunion between Christ and His followers.

    > "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
    *   *Key Theme:* The manner of His return will be physical and visible, just as His departure was.

### 2. The Epistles (Letters to the Churches)
The apostles wrote to early Christians to clarify the nature of the return and to encourage them to live holy lives in anticipation of it.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the final judgment?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 25:31-46, Rev 20:11-15, 2 Cor 5:10, Acts 17:31
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the final judgment in numerous places throughout both the Old and New Testaments. While the specific details vary, the consistent message is that God will ultimately judge the world in righteousness, holding all people accountable for their actions, words, and hearts.

Here are the key passages where the Bible teaches about the final judgment, categorized by their focus:

### 1. The Great White Throne Judgment (Revelation 20)
This is the most detailed and famous description of the final judgment in the Bible. It describes the resurrection of the dead and the legal proceeding before God.

*   **Revelation 20:11–15:** "Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it... And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Another book was opened, which is the book of life. The dead were judged according to what they had done as recorded in the books... Anyone whose name was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire."

### 2. The Teachings of Jesus
Jesus spoke frequently about judgment, emphasizing that it would be based on one's relationship with Him and how they treated others.

*   **Matthew 25:31–46 (The Sheep and the Goats):** Jesus describes the Son of Man sitting on his throne in heavenly glory, separating the nations like a shepherd separates sheep from goats. The "righteous" inherit the kingdom, while others depart to eternal punishment. The criteria is surprisingly practical: how they treated the hungry, the stranger, the sick, and the imprisoned ("the least of these").
*   **John 5:22, 26-29:** Jesus states, "Moreover, the Father judges no one, but has entrusted all judgment to the Son... for a time is coming when all who are in their graves will hear his voice and come out—those who have done what is good will rise to live, and those who have done what is evil will rise to be condemned."
*   **Matthew 12:36:** "But I tell you that everyone will have to give account on the day of judgment for every empty word they have spoken."

### 3. The Apostolic Teachings (Paul and Peter)
The apostles reinforced that judgment is universal (affecting believers and unbelievers) and inescapable.

*   **Romans 2:5–6:** Paul warns against a stubborn heart, writing, "But because of your stubbornness and your unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of God’s wrath, when his righteous judgment will be revealed. God 'will repay each person according to what they have done.'"
*   **2 Corinthians 5:10:** "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive what is due us for the things done while in the body, whether good or bad."
*   **Hebrews 9:27:** This verse establishes the timeline of human existence: "Just as people are destined to die once, and after that to face judgment."
*   **2 Peter 3:7:** Peter explains that the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, "being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men."

### 4. Old Testament Foundations
The concept of a final divine judgment is rooted in the Old Testament prophets, who looked forward to a day when God would set all wrongs right.

*   **Daniel 7:9–10:** Daniel sees a vision of "Ancient of Days" taking his seat. "The court was seated, and the books were opened." This imagery is the foundation for the New Testament depiction in Revelation.
*   **Ecclesiastes 12:14:** "For God will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil."

### Summary of Key Themes
Across these varied texts, the Bible teaches four consistent truths about the final judgment:

1.  **Certainty:** It is an appointed event that will definitely happen.
2.  **Universality:** All humanity—living and dead—will stand before

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about heaven and hell?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rev 21:1-4, Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, John 14:2-3
questions.response:
The Bible describes heaven and hell not merely as places of destination, but as states of existence defined by the presence or absence of God. While the Old Testament focuses heavily on *Sheol* (the grave or realm of the dead), the New Testament provides a much clearer revelation of the afterlife through the teachings of Jesus and the Apostles.

Here is a categorized list of key Scripture passages regarding heaven and hell.

### I. Biblical Teaching on Heaven

The Bible describes heaven as a place of joy, worship, and the presence of God. It is often referred to as "Paradise" or the "Father’s House."

**1. The Dwelling Place of God**
*   **Matthew 6:9:** "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name." (Jesus teaches that heaven is the Father's location).
*   **Psalm 103:19:** "The Lord has established his throne in heaven, and his kingdom rules over all."

**2. The Hope of the Resurrection and Eternal Life**
*   **John 14:1–3:** "Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. My Father’s house has many rooms; if that were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am."
*   **Philippians 1:21–23:** "For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain... I am torn between the two: I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is better by far."
*   **2 Corinthians 5:1–8:** Paul speaks of an "eternal house in heaven" and says that to be "absent from the body" is to be "present with the Lord."

**3. The New Heaven and New Earth (The Final State)**
*   **Revelation 21:1–4:** "Then I saw 'a new heaven and a new earth,' for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away... He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away."
*   **Revelation 22:1–5:** Describes the river of life and the tree of life, noting that "there will be no more night" and God’s servants will reign forever.

**4. Rewards and Joy**
*   **Matthew 5:12:** "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven."
*   **Psalm 16:11:** "You make known to me the path of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence, with eternal pleasures at your right hand."

---

The Bible describes hell as a place of judgment, separation from God, and destruction. The New Testament uses specific Greek words: *Hades* (the realm of the dead) and *Gehenna* (a place of final punishment, named after the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem).

**1. Described as "Gehenna" and Unquenchable Fire**
*   **Mark 9:43–48:** Jesus warns: "It is better for you to enter life maimed than with two hands to go into hell [Gehenna], where the fire never goes out... where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched."

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of creation?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 1:1, John 1:3, Col 1:16, Heb 11:3
questions.response:
The Bible teaches the doctrine of creation across both the Old and New Testaments. While the narrative of creation begins in Genesis, the biblical authors throughout Scripture reflect on what creation means, who the Creator is, and humanity's place within it.

Here is a breakdown of where the Bible teaches the doctrine of creation, organized by theological themes.

### 1. The Narrative Account: God as the Originator
The most obvious place to start is the opening book of the Bible, which provides the foundational narrative.

*   **Genesis 1:1–2:3:** This is the primary text, often called the "Cosmic Temple" narrative. It teaches that God created the heavens and the earth *ex nihilo* (out of nothing). It establishes a pattern of order coming out of chaos, culminating in the Sabbath rest.
    *   *Key theme:* God speaks, and it happens (Divine Fiat). The repeated phrase "And God saw that it was good" establishes the inherent value of the material world.
*   **Genesis 2:4–25:** This is a second, more intimate account focusing on the creation of humanity (Adam and Eve). It emphasizes that God formed man from the dust and breathed life into him.
    *   *Key theme:* God is personal and relational; humanity is given stewardship over the garden.

### 2. The Wisdom Literature: Creation by Wisdom
The poetic books of the Bible (Psalms, Proverbs, Job) move beyond the "how" to the "why." They teach that creation is not random, but the result of God’s wisdom and skill.

*   **Proverbs 8:22–31:** Personified Wisdom is described as being present with God at creation, acting as a "master craftsman." This suggests creation is not an accident but an intentional, wise design.
*   **Psalm 104:** This Psalm is often called a "creation hymn." It retells the Genesis 1 account poetically, showing how God actively sustains creation—providing water for animals, causing grass to grow, and appointing the moon for seasons.
*   **Psalm 139:13–14:** Focuses on the creation of the individual, stating, "You knit me together in my mother’s womb." This teaches that God’s creative work is ongoing and personal.
*   **Job 38–41:** When Job questions God’s justice, God answers by pointing to His power in creation. He asks Job, "Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundation?" This passage teaches that the Creator’s wisdom is far superior to human understanding.

### 3. The Prophets: The Uniqueness of the Creator
The prophets often use creation to contrast the God of Israel with the idols of surrounding nations.

*   **Isaiah 40:25–26:** "Lift up your eyes and look to the heavens: Who created all these?" God is contrasted with idols because He is the one who brings out the starry host one by one.
*   **Isaiah 45:18:** "For this is what the Lord says—he who created the heavens, he is God; he who fashioned and made the earth, he founded it; he did not create it to be empty, but formed it to be inhabited." This reinforces that creation has a purpose.

### 4. The New Testament: Creation through Christ
The New Testament radically reframes the doctrine of creation by revealing that Jesus Christ was the agent of creation.

*   **John 1:1–3:** "In the beginning was the Word... Through him all things were made; without him, nothing was made that has been made." This identifies Jesus (the Word) as the Creator God, present at Genesis 1:1.
*   **Colossians 1:15–17:** Paul writes that "by him [Jesus] all things were created: things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible... all things were created through him and for him." This teaches that creation is Christ-centered—it exists for Him.
*   **Hebrews 1:2:** States that in these last days, God has spoken

questions.question: What passages teach about God's providence?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 10:29-31, Rom 8:28, Eph 1:11, Dan 4:35
questions.response:
The Bible teaches that God’s providence is His divine guidance and care over His creation. It is the doctrine that God did not just create the world and leave it to run on its own, but is actively involved in sustaining, governing, and directing all things according to His holy will.

Here are key passages that teach about God's providence, categorized by theme.

### 1. God’s Sovereign Control Over All Events
These passages establish that God is in control of history and the big picture of the universe.

*   **Daniel 4:35** – "All the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, 'What have you done?'"
    *   *Teaching:* God’s will is unstoppable; no human or angelic power can thwart His plans.
*   **Isaiah 46:9–11** – "I am God, and there is no other... declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, ‘My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.’"
    *   *Teaching:* God predicts the future because He ordains it. His plans cannot fail.
*   **Ephesians 1:11** – "In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will."
    *   *Teaching:* God is not reacting to history; He is actively working *all things* (not just some things) according to His purpose.

### 2. God’s Care for the Details (The "Micro" View)
Providence is not just about empires and nations; it extends to the smallest details of life and nature.

*   **Matthew 10:29–31** – "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows."
    *   *Teaching:* God’s governance extends to the death of a common bird and the number of hairs on a head. This provides comfort that He watches over His children intimately.
*   **Proverbs 16:33** – "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord."
    *   *Teaching:* Even events that appear random (like rolling dice or a "lucky" break) are under God’s sovereign control.
*   **Psalm 139:16** – "Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them."
    *   *Teaching:* God’s providence covers the length and details of our lives before we are even born.

### 3. Providence Over Human Decisions and Evil
One of the most complex aspects of providence is how God can be in control while humans make free choices, including sinful ones. The Bible teaches that God can use even evil actions to accomplish His good purposes without being the author of the sin.

*   **Genesis 50:20** – (Joseph speaking to his brothers) "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today."
    *   *Teaching:* The brothers were morally responsible for their sin (they meant evil), but God had a concurrent purpose (He meant it for good). God’s providence turns evil into salvation.
*   **Acts 2:23** – "This Jesus

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the nature and practice of prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Phil 4:6, 1 Thess 5:17, John 14:13-14
questions.response:
Scripture addresses the nature and practice of prayer extensively, weaving it through both the Old and New Testaments. Rather than isolating prayer to a single chapter, the Bible presents it as the fundamental lifeline of the relationship between God and humanity.

Here is a thematic overview of where Scripture teaches about the nature and practice of prayer.

### 1. The Model Prayer: The "Lord’s Prayer"
The most comprehensive single teaching on the *practice* of prayer comes from Jesus Himself. In response to the disciples' request, "Lord, teach us to pray" (Luke 11:1), Jesus provides a template that outlines the priorities of prayer.

*   **Matthew 6:9–13 & Luke 11:2–4:** This passage outlines the proper structure:
    *   **Relationship:** "Our Father in heaven" (Intimacy combined with reverence).
    *   **Reverence:** "Hallowed be your name" (Worship comes first).
    *   **Submission:** "Your kingdom come, your will be done" (Aligning human will with Divine will).
    *   **Dependence:** "Give us this day our daily bread" (Trusting God for physical needs).
    *   **Confession:** "Forgive us our debts" (Acknowledging sin).
    *   **Deliverance:** "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Spiritual protection).

### 2. The Attitude of the Heart (The Nature of Prayer)
Scripture emphasizes that the *nature* of prayer is not about external ritual or eloquent words, but the posture of the heart.

*   **Humility vs. Hypocrisy:**
    *   **Luke 18:9–14 (The Pharisee and the Tax Collector):** Jesus contrasts a self-righteous prayer with a humble one. The conclusion is that "everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted." This teaches that God hears the broken spirit, not the boastful spirit.
    *   **Matthew 6:5–8:** Jesus warns against praying to be seen by others ("standing in the synagogues") and against "heaping up empty phrases" (vain repetition). The nature of prayer is secret, sincere, and simple.

*   **Faith:**

questions.question: What Bible passages relate to Sabbath observance?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:8-11, Isa 58:13-14, Mark 2:27-28, Heb 4:9-10
questions.response:
The Bible contains numerous passages regarding the Sabbath, ranging from its establishment in Creation to its observance in the Mosaic Law, critiques by the Prophets, and its interpretation in the New Testament.

Here is a categorized list of key Bible passages relating to Sabbath observance.

### 1. The Origin and Pattern of the Sabbath
These passages establish the Sabbath as a divine institution.

*   **Genesis 2:2–3:** The first mention of the Sabbath. God rests on the seventh day after Creation, blessing and sanctifying it. This establishes the pattern of a seven-day week.
*   **Exodus 16:23–30:** Before the Ten Commandments were given, this passage describes the collection of manna. The Israelites are commanded to gather a double portion on the sixth day because the seventh day is "a solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the Lord."

### 2. The Sabbath in the Law (The Torah)
The Sabbath is central to the Mosaic Covenant and is enshrined in the Ten Commandments.

*   **Exodus 20:8–11:** The Fourth Commandment. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy." The motivation here is theological: remembering God's creation.
*   **Deuteronomy 5:12–15:** The restatement of the Fourth Commandment. Here, the motivation is social and redemptive: remembering that they were slaves in Egypt and that God delivered them.
*   **Exodus 31:12–17:** This passage defines the Sabbath as a "sign" between God and the Israelites "throughout your generations." It emphasizes the severity of the command (whoever profanes it shall be cut off) and the concept of it being a perpetual covenant.
*   **Exodus 35:2–3:** Specific instructions that no work should be done and notably, "You shall kindle no fire in all your dwelling places on the Sabbath day."
*   **Numbers 15:32–36:** A narrative example of a man caught gathering sticks on the Sabbath and the subsequent divine instruction to stone him, illustrating the strictness of the law in the Old Testament theocracy.
*   **Leviticus 23:3:** The Sabbath is listed first among the appointed feasts of the Lord, described as a day of "holy convocation" (a gathering for worship).

### 3. The Sabbath in the Prophets
The prophets often rebuked Israel for neglecting the Sabbath and promised blessings for its observance.

*   **Isaiah 58:13–14:** A classic passage on the *spirit* of the Sabbath. It promises that if the people call the Sabbath a "delight" and honor it by not going their own way, they will find joy in the Lord.
*   **Jeremiah 17:21–27:** A warning against carrying burdens in and out of Jerusalem on the Sabbath. It contrasts the consequences of disobedience (fire in the gates of Jerusalem) with obedience (kings riding in chariots through the gates).
*   **Ezekiel 20:12–24:** God recounts how He gave the Sabbaths to Israel as a sign, but the people rebelled and profaned it by not walking in His statutes.
*   **Amos 8:5:** A critique of merchants who were impatient for the Sabbath to end so they could cheat customers ("When will the Sabbath be past, that we may sell wheat?").

### 4. The Sabbath in the New Testament (Gospels)
Jesus had frequent conflicts with religious leaders over Sabbath observance, redefining its purpose.

*   **Mark 2:23–28 (cf. Matthew 12:1–8; Luke 6:1–5):** The disciples pluck grain on the Sabbath. Jesus defends them by citing David eating the showbread and declares, *"The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath."* He concludes, *"The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath."*
*   **Matthew 12:9–14 (cf. Mark 3:1–6; Luke 13:10–17):** Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath. He argues that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, using the analogy of rescuing a sheep that has fallen into a pit.

questions.question: Where are the Ten Commandments given in Scripture?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:1-17, Deut 5:6-21
questions.response:
The Ten Commandments are recorded in two primary passages in the Bible:

**1. Exodus 20:1–17**
This is the original giving of the Law. Moses leads the Israelites to Mount Sinai, where God speaks these commandments to the people and writes them on two tablets of stone.

**2. Deuteronomy 5:4–21**
This is the second giving of the Law. Forty years later, as the Israelites prepare to enter the Promised Land, Moses recounts the commandments to the new generation of Israelites.

While the commandments are the same in both passages, there are slight variations in the wording, most notably in the reasoning given for the **Fourth Commandment** (keeping the Sabbath):
*   **In Exodus:** The Sabbath is kept as a memorial of God's rest after creation.
*   **In Deuteronomy:** The Sabbath is kept as a remembrance of the Israelites' deliverance from slavery in Egypt.

questions.question: Where does Jesus teach the Lord's Prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Luke 11:2-4
questions.response:
Jesus teaches the Lord's Prayer in two different books of the New Testament: the **Gospel of Matthew** and the **Gospel of Luke**.

Here are the specific locations and contexts for each:

**1. The Gospel of Matthew (Matthew 6:9–13)**
This is the more familiar and longer version of the prayer, often used in church liturgy. It is found within the **Sermon on the Mount**. Here, Jesus teaches the prayer as part of a broader instruction on how not to pray (like the hypocrites or pagans) and how to pray correctly.

**2. The Gospel of Luke (Luke 11:2–4)**
This version is shorter and occurs in a different setting. Jesus is praying in a certain place, and when he finishes, one of his disciples asks him, *"Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples."* In response, Jesus provides the prayer.

**Key Differences:**
While the core sentiments are the same, Matthew’s version includes the opening "Our Father in heaven" and the concluding doxology ("For thine is the kingdom..."), whereas Luke’s version is more concise, simply beginning with "Father."

questions.question: What passages address the sacraments in Reformed theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4
questions.response:
In Reformed theology, the sacraments are viewed as "signs and seals" of God's grace and the promises of the Gospel. They are means of grace that strengthen the believer's faith, but they are not automatically effective apart from faith and the working of the Holy Spirit.

To understand the Reformed view, one must look at three categories of passages: **The Confessional Standards** (the definitive theological documents), **John Calvin’s Institutes** (the systematic exposition), and **Key Scriptural Texts** (the biblical foundation).

Here are the key passages addressing the sacraments in Reformed theology.

### 1. The Confessional Standards
These documents define the orthodoxy of Reformed churches (Presbyterian and Continental Reformed).

**The Westminster Confession of Faith (Chapter 27)**
This is the most precise systematic definition of a sacrament in the Reformed tradition.
*   **WCF 27.1:** Defines sacraments as "holy signs and seals of the covenant of grace, immediately instituted by God, to represent Christ and his benefits; and to confirm our interest in him: as also, to put a visible difference between those that belong unto the church and the rest of the world; and solemnly to engage them to the service of God in Christ, according to his Word."
*   **WCF 27.3:** Explains the efficacy: "The grace which is exhibited in or by the sacraments rightly used, is not conferred by any power in them; neither doth the efficacy of a sacrament depend upon the piety or intention of him that doth administer it: but upon the work of the Spirit, and the word of institution."

**The Heidelberg Catechism (Lord’s Days 25–30)**
This document is more pastoral and devotional in tone, widely used in the Continental Reformed tradition.
*   **Q&A 66:** "What are the sacraments? The sacraments are visible holy signs and seals appointed by God for this end, that by their use He may the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the Gospel."
*   **Q&A 67:** "Are both the Word and the sacraments designed to direct our faith to the sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross as the only ground of our salvation? Yes, truly."

**The Belgic Confession (Articles 33–35)**
*   **Article 33:** Discusses the sacraments generally, stating that God "added" them to the Word to "nourish and sustain" the church, comparing them to "visible signs" like wedding rings that seal a promise.

### 2. John Calvin’s Institutes of the Christian Religion
John Calvin is the primary architect of Reformed sacramental theology. His treatment in *The Institutes* is essential reading.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about church discipline?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 18:15-17, 1 Cor 5:1-13, Titus 3:10, 2 Thess 3:14-15
questions.response:
The Bible’s teaching on church discipline is primarily found in the New Testament. It is presented not as a means of punishment or cruelty, but as a method of restoration, protection, and maintaining the purity of the church.

Here are the key passages where the Bible teaches about church discipline, categorized by how they address the issue.

### 1. The Primary Procedure: Matthew 18:15–17
This is the most foundational text for the process of church discipline. Jesus outlines a step-by-step approach for dealing with a believer who is caught in sin.

*   **Step 1 (Private confrontation):** "If your brother or sister sins, go and point out their fault, just between the two of you." The goal is to win them over privately.
*   **Step 2 (Small group witness):** If they refuse to listen, "take one or two others along, so that 'every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.'"
*   **Step 3 (Church involvement):** If they still refuse to listen, "tell it to the church."
*   **Step 4 (Exclusion):** If they refuse to listen even to the church, "treat them as you would a pagan or a tax collector" (implying a break in fellowship or membership).

### 2. The Purpose and Severity: 1 Corinthians 5
In this chapter, Paul addresses a specific case of sexual immorality in the Corinthian church. He teaches why discipline is necessary and how it should be enacted.

*   **The Command to Remove:** Paul instructs the church to "hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord" (v. 5). This shows the ultimate goal is **redemption** (saving the spirit), even if the method is severe.
*   **The Analogy of Leaven:** Paul uses the metaphor of yeast working through dough (v. 6–8). He argues that allowing open sin to remain in the church will eventually corrupt the whole community ("a little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough").
*   **The Scope:** Paul clarifies that this judgment applies to those *inside* the church, not to non-believers (v. 12–13). The famous phrase "Expel the wicked person from among you" concludes the passage.

### 3. The Heart and Spirit of Discipline: Galatians 6:1
This verse provides the necessary attitude required for those administering discipline.

*   **Restoration:** "Brothers and sisters, if someone is caught in a sin, you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently."
*   **Humility:** The text warns the restorer to "watch yourselves, or you also may be tempted." Discipline must be done with a spirit of gentleness and self-awareness, not arrogance.

### 4. Dealing with Divisive People: Titus 3:10–11
Paul gives specific instructions regarding those who cause division rather than moral failure.

*   **The Process:** "Warn a divisive person once, and then warn them a second time. After that, have nothing to do with them."
*   **The Reason:** Such a person is "warped and sinful; they are self-condemned." This suggests a quicker process for those who threaten the unity of the church.

### 5. Withdrawing from Idleness: 2 Thessalonians 3:6–15
Paul addresses believers who are idle and disruptive, refusing to work.

*   **The Action:** "Keep away from every believer who is idle and disruptive."
*   **The Nuance:** Paul clarifies, "Do not regard them as an enemy, but warn them as a fellow believer." This distinguishes church discipline from shunning an enemy; the relationship remains corrective, not hostile.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about Christian liberty?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gal 5:1, 1 Cor 8:9, Rom 14:1-23, 1 Pet 2:16
questions.response:
The Bible teaches that Christian liberty (or freedom) is a central benefit of the Gospel. However, Scripture presents a nuanced view: believers are freed *from* the penalty and power of sin, but they are freed *to* serve God and love others.

Here are the key Scripture passages regarding Christian liberty, categorized by their specific teaching.

### 1. The Source and Nature of Liberty
These passages establish that freedom is not achieved through human effort, but is a gift purchased by Christ.

*   **Galatians 5:1**
    > *"It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery."*
    *   This is the "Magna Carta" of Christian liberty. Paul warns the Galatians not to return to the slavery of legalism (trying to earn salvation through the law).
*   **John 8:31–32, 36**
    > *"So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."*
    *   Jesus defines true freedom as freedom from sin. It is not political or libertarian freedom, but spiritual liberation.
*   **Romans 8:1–2**
    > *"Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, because through Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit who gives life has set you free from the law of sin and death."*
    *   Liberty begins with the removal of condemnation. The Christian is free from the guilt that the law produces.

### 2. Freedom from the Law
A significant aspect of Christian liberty is freedom from the ceremonial and civil laws of the Old Covenant, as well as the burden of man-made religious rules.

*   **Colossians 2:16–17**
    > *"Therefore do not let anyone judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a religious festival, a New Moon celebration or a Sabbath day. These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ."*
    *   Paul teaches that believers are not bound by dietary restrictions or religious calendars. These were shadows pointing to Jesus; now that Jesus has come, the shadow is no longer binding.
*   **Acts 15:10–11**
    > *"Now then, why do you try to test God by putting on the necks of Gentiles a yoke that neither we nor our ancestors have been able to bear? No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are."*
    *   At the Jerusalem Council, the apostles determined that Gentile converts did not need to follow the full Mosaic Law to be saved.

### 3. Freedom of Conscience (Adiaphora)

*   **Romans 14:1–4, 14**

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about marriage?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 2:24, Eph 5:22-33, Matt 19:4-6, Heb 13:4
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about marriage from the very beginning of Genesis to the end of Revelation. It presents marriage not merely as a social contract, but as a divine institution created by God.

Here is a breakdown of the key locations in Scripture where marriage is defined, instructed, and illustrated.

### 1. The Institution of Marriage (Genesis)
The foundational teaching on marriage is found in the creation account. Here, marriage is defined as a heterosexual, monogamous union.

*   **Genesis 2:18–24:** This is the "blueprint" for marriage.
    *   **Companionship:** It begins with God saying, "It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a helper suitable for him" (v. 18). Marriage is intended to solve human isolation.
    *   **Unity:** The text famously says, "That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh" (v. 24). This establishes the principle of **leaving** (prioritizing the new family), **cleaving** (commitment), and **weaving** (intimacy/one-flesh).
*   **Genesis 1:27–28:** This passage establishes the **procreative** purpose of marriage ("Be fruitful and increase in number") and the **complementarity** of the sexes ("male and female he created them").

### 2. Jesus’ Teaching on Marriage (The Gospels)
Jesus reaffirms the Genesis definition of marriage and raises the standard regarding permanence.

*   **Matthew 19:3–6 (and Mark 10:6–9):** When asked about divorce, Jesus quotes Genesis 2:24. He teaches that marriage is God’s doing ("what God has joined together"), not just a human arrangement. He emphasizes that the "one flesh" union makes the husband and wife one person, implying that separation is a violation of God's creative intent.
*   **John 2:1–11:** Jesus performs his first miracle at a wedding in Cana, signaling his approval of the marriage celebration and institution.

### 3. The Mystery of Marriage (The Epistles)
The New Testament letters provide practical instructions for husbands and wives and reveal the theological purpose of marriage.

*   **Ephesians 5:22–33:** This is perhaps the most significant New Testament passage on marriage. Paul gives specific roles:
    *   **Wives:** Called to respect and submit to their husbands as the church submits to Christ.
    *   **Husbands:** Called to love their wives as Christ loved the church—sacrificially and selflessly.
    *   **The Theology:** Paul reveals that human marriage is a metaphor (a "mystery") meant to illustrate the relationship between Christ and the Church.
*   **1 Corinthians 7:** This chapter is entirely dedicated to questions about marriage and singleness. Paul addresses:
    *   Sexual relations within marriage (husband and wife have authority over each other's bodies).
    *   The value of singleness for undivided devotion to the Lord.
    *   Instructions for mixed-faith marriages (believers married to non-believers).
*   **Colossians 3:18–19 & 1 Peter 3:1–7:** These passages offer shorter, practical "household codes," reiterating the call for wives to be submissive and husbands to be loving and understanding.

### 4. Wisdom Literature (Old Testament)
The wisdom books of the Old Testament offer practical advice on the daily life of marriage.

*   **Proverbs 18:22:** "He who finds a wife finds what is good and receives favor from the Lord." (Marriage as a blessing).
*   **Proverbs 31:** Describes the "wife of noble character," showing a marriage where the wife is an industrious, wise, and respected partner.
*   **Song of Solomon:** This book is a poetic celebration of romantic love, desire, and sexual intimacy within marriage. It counters the idea that physical intimacy is purely for procreation; it is also for joy and pleasure.

### 5. The Ultimate Symbol (Revelation)
At the end of the Bible, marriage is used as the primary metaphor for the end of human history.

*   **Revelation 19:7–9 & 21:2:** The Bible concludes with the "Wedding Supper of the Lamb." Here, the relationship between God and his redeemed people is finalized like a wedding. This reinforces the idea that earthly marriage is a temporary pointer toward the eternal reality of union with God.

### Summary of Biblical Themes
Across these texts, the Bible teaches three main purposes for marriage:
1.  **Companionship:** To alleviate loneliness (Genesis 2).
2.  **Procreation:** To raise godly offspring (Genesis 1; Malachi 2:15).
3.  **Christlikeness:** To sanctify the partners and display the gospel (Ephesians 5).

questions.question: What passages address the role of the civil magistrate?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 13:1-7, 1 Pet 2:13-17, Acts 5:29, Dan 2:21
questions.response:
The Bible addresses the role of the civil magistrate (government leaders, kings, judges, and rulers) primarily through two lenses: their **divine appointment** and their **specific duties** regarding justice and order.

Here are the key passages categorized by theme.

### 1. The Divine Institution of Authority
These passages establish that government is not a human invention but an institution ordained by God.

*   **Romans 13:1–2 (ESV)**
    > "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment."
    *   *Key Principle:* All authority is delegated by God; therefore, resisting authority is, in principle, resisting God.

*   **John 19:10–11 (ESV)**
    > "So Pilate said to him, 'You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?' Jesus answered him, 'You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above...'"
    *   *Key Principle:* Even an unrighteous ruler like Pilate possesses authority only because it was "given" to him from above.

*   **Daniel 2:21 (ESV)**
    > "He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings..."
    *   *Key Principle:* God is sovereign over the rise and fall of political leaders.

### 2. The Purpose of the Magistrate: Justice and Order
The Bible defines the "job description" of a ruler as one who punishes evil and praises good.

*   **Romans 13:3–4 (ESV)**
    > "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer."
    *   *Key Principle:* The primary role of the state is to restrain evil ("the sword") and protect those who do good. The magistrate is called a "servant of God" (diakonos).

*   **1 Peter 2:13–14 (ESV)**
    > "Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good."
    *   *Key Principle:* Rulers are "sent" by God with a specific mandate: to punish evildoers and commend those who do right.

### 3. The Responsibility to Judge Righteously
In the Old Testament, the standard for a magistrate was strict adherence to justice, specifically protecting the vulnerable.

*   **Deuteronomy 16:18–20 (ESV)**
    > "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns that the Lord your God is giving you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment. You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality, and you shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous. Justice, and only justice, you shall follow..."
    *   *Key Principle:* Magistrates must be impartial, refuse bribes, and pursue justice relentlessly.

*   **2 Samuel 23:3–4 (ESV)**
    > "He who rules over men righteously, ruling in the fear of God, is like the light of morning when the sun rises, a morning without clouds..."
    *   *Key Principle:* A good ruler governs with righteousness and the "fear of God."

*   **Proverbs 31:8–9 (ESV)**
    > "Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy."
    *   *Key Principle:* The magistrate has a duty to advocate for those who cannot speak for themselves.
